title: Good Pope John (1958–1963)
hook: a farmer's son, warm and brave, whose letter on peace was addressed to all people of goodwill

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pier Giorgio Frassati, who wrote verso l'alto, the student who climbed mountains and quietly visited the poor. Your line was to the heights. What did you climb, a hill or a staircase? Today, a pope the people of Rome simply called good. Day nine hundred seventeen.

A letter from a pope usually opens by saying who it is for. The bishops. The clergy. The faithful. This one does all that, and then it keeps going. It is addressed, its opening says, to all men of good will. Not only Catholics. Not only believers. Anyone who means well, wherever they are. The man who signed it had grown up in a farming family in the hills of northern Italy, and he never lost the manner of a country priest: jokes, plain talk, a big laugh. People in Rome gave him a plainer name. Good Pope John.
screen: `A LETTER WITH A WIDE ADDRESS.` → `A FARMING FAMILY.` → `GOOD POPE JOHN.`

segments.voice: His name was Angelo Roncalli, and as pope he took the name John. Four things about him. First, the farm. He came from a family that worked the land, and he wrote about that childhood with affection in his spiritual diary, later published as Journal of a Soul. He did not pretend to be grander than he was. Second, the window. He surprised the Church by calling a council, a gathering of the world's bishops in Rome, which became the Second Vatican Council. Tradition says he described it as opening a window to let in fresh air. What that council changed in ordinary parishes is tomorrow's story. Third, the letter. As pope he wrote an encyclical called Pacem in Terris, Latin for peace on earth. It says that peace among nations has to stand on four things: truth, justice, love and freedom. It speaks of the rights every human being has simply by being human, and the duties that come with them. And it was addressed not only to Catholics but to all people of good will. Fourth, the echo. That phrase has an old sound for Catholics. On the night of Christ's birth, Luke's Gospel says, the angels sang, in the Douay-Rheims, "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will." A pope borrowing the angels' address for a letter about peace. It was his way of saying that the work of peace is shared with anyone willing to do it.
screen: `A FARMER'S SON NAMED ANGELO.` · `HE OPENS A WINDOW: A COUNCIL.` · `PEACE ON TRUTH, JUSTICE, LOVE, FREEDOM.` · `THE ANGELS' ADDRESS, BORROWED.` · then, large: `ON EARTH PEACE TO MEN OF GOOD WILL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write, in your head first, to someone of goodwill. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who means well, maybe someone you disagree with about a lot, but whose good intentions you trust. A neighbor, a coworker, a relative across a political line. Let one honest sentence form: thank you for something, or I see what you're trying to do. Keep it short and true. If you pray, you can pray the angels' line from Luke for them. If you don't, simply hold them in mind and wish them well. After the bell, send it. The bell holds the time.
Angelo Roncalli. The farmer's son who became pope, took the name John, called the Second Vatican Council, and wrote Pacem in Terris to all people of good will.

Your line: all people of goodwill. This week ran from Titus Brandsma and Irena Sendler through Dorothy Day, Peter Maurin, Gianna Beretta Molla and Pier Giorgio Frassati, to Good Pope John. Today, send that one message. Day nine hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Catholics remember Saint John XXIII on his feast day, and Pacem in Terris is still read in Catholic schools, parishes and peace groups as a foundation of the Church's teaching on peace and human rights.

fork.setup: you're Pope John, writing a letter about peace in a tense world. who do you address it to?
fork.reveal: after the bishops and the faithful, he added all people of good will, borrowing the angels' address from Luke.

original.note: Latin: peace on earth, the opening words that give the encyclical its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pope's letter is written for Catholics only.
what it means: Pacem in Terris was addressed to all people of good will, believers or not.
what a scholar hears: the Latin address, men of good will, uses the angels' words from Luke 2:14 in the Vulgate.
